clue.text: Pocket-money earned immorally, by implication?

parts.note: small change in the pocket, re-read as money gained by someone of easy morals

explanation.surface: A question about where a child's pocket money really came from.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for spare change is read literally: LOOSE can mean immoral, so the cash is what a loose person earns.
explanation.definitionFit: Coins carried in a pocket rather than notes or a wallet are the standard phrase for small change.

clue.text: Reputedly marvellous little ruler

parts.note: a fabled (so only reputedly real) and wonderful king of the little people, the fairies

explanation.surface: A small monarch said to be wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little ruler' suggests a short king or a small measuring stick; it is the king of the fairies in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, a creature of fable.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare and folklore the fairy king, husband of Titania, is a magical sovereign of tiny beings.

clue.text: A comparison I show amusement about

indicators.note: about means going round, so one piece encloses the other here

parts.note: to show amusement is to smile

explanation.surface: Someone grins at a comparison they find funny.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure of speech likening one thing to another with 'like' or 'as' is the textbook kind of comparison.

clue.text: Monument erected for troops sent to fight on a narrow front

definitions.meaning: a tall pillar put up as a memorial, like Nelson's in Trafalgar Square

definitions.text: troops sent to fight on a narrow front
definitions.meaning: a military formation that is long and only a few soldiers wide

explanation.surface: A memorial put up for soldiers who fought in a tight battle line.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a memorial pillar and a narrow, deep formation of soldiers share the one word for a vertical or lengthwise file.

clue.text: But it's not at all the sort of stuff one would get from a game-dealer!

definitions.text: But it's not at all the sort of stuff one would get from a game-dealer!

parts.words: But it's not at all the sort of stuff one would get from a game-dealer
parts.note: a game-dealer sells pheasant and venison, but read as a dealer in games it suggests bats, balls and rackets

explanation.surface: A remark that a game dealer's shop would never stock this.
explanation.walkthrough: A game-dealer in Britain sells shot birds and deer; the clue denies he sells kit for games, playing on 'game' as hunted meat versus sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Rackets, balls, bats and nets are the gear used for playing games and athletics.

clue.text: A quadruped that's particularly good at drawing out of 15, maybe

definitions.text: A quadruped that's particularly good at drawing

indicators.note: made out of the letters of the other entry, which are rearranged to give this word

parts.note: the answer to 15 down, a word for a band of players

explanation.surface: An animal with a talent for sketching, drawn from an orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawing' suggests art, but the beast draws carts. 'out of ... maybe' rearranges the letters of 15 down.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy draught animal bred to pull wagons is a four-legged beast whose job is hauling loads.

clue.text: Equally sure to get at the truth?

parts.note: as, as in 'as good', means to the same degree
certain is a synonym of sure

explanation.surface: Being equally sure as a route to finding out what really happened.
explanation.definitionFit: To find out for certain is to establish the facts of a matter.

clue.text: Can somehow repent about what the relevant facts are

indicators.note: about places the rearranged letters round the other piece
somehow says the letters of repent are to be arranged in some new way

parts.note: a tin is a can

explanation.surface: Someone can repent once they know the relevant facts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb (is able to) but is the noun for a tin; 'somehow' and 'about' do the shuffling and enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: Facts that are relevant are apposite and bear directly on the matter.

clue.text: A fool put into the draw for the Scottish junior cup

indicators.note: put into means set inside, so one piece goes in the middle of the other

parts.note: a tie is a drawn game
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: A fool is entered into the draw for a Scottish youth football competition.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a cup draw in junior football; in Scots a small drinking cup is a tassie.
explanation.definitionFit: Scots dialect uses this word for a little drinking cup, junior meaning small.

clue.text: Red lubricant turned into noxious fauna

indicators.note: into says the turned piece goes inside the other

parts.note: vermin are harmful animals such as rats

indicators.note: turned means the word for lubricant is read backwards

parts.note: oil is a lubricant

explanation.surface: Red oil spilt among pests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' makes LIO from OIL, which goes 'into' VERMIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A brilliant scarlet pigment is one of the classic named shades of red.

clue.text: Speak on oath at trial

parts.note: a test is a trial

explanation.surface: Giving sworn evidence in court.
explanation.definitionFit: To declare something true as a witness under oath is to bear witness formally.

clue.text: Easy victory for any women who has a silly husband?

definitions.meaning: the quickest possible checkmate in chess, won in two moves

definitions.text: any women who has a silly husband
definitions.meaning: the wife or partner of an idiot

explanation.surface: A wife married to a fool wins without trying.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess term for the two-move checkmate also reads as the spouse of a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess the fastest checkmate is a trivial win; read literally, the phrase is an idiot's spouse.

clue.text: The cotton town that doesn't operate an open-door policy?

definitions.text: The cotton town that doesn't operate an open-door policy?

parts.words: The cotton town that doesn't operate an open-door policy
parts.note: a Lancashire mill town, whose name split in two describes a door kept fastened

explanation.surface: A northern mill town that is unwelcoming to outsiders.
explanation.walkthrough: BOLTON is a Lancashire town known for cotton mills; split as BOLT ON it describes a door bolted shut.
explanation.definitionFit: A Greater Manchester town that grew on cotton spinning, whose name split in two means a door kept secured.

clue.text: Unbiased aim

explanation.definitionFit: The one word means both impartial and a goal one is working towards.

clue.text: A band or box finished off by an artist

indicators.note: finished off by means the last piece comes at the end

parts.note: taken as written
a chest is a box
RA, Royal Academician, is the usual crossword artist

explanation.surface: A band or a box completed by a painter.
explanation.definitionFit: A large group of musicians playing together is a band.

clue.text: He can always crack the whip if a wild-cat strike is 0 threatened

definitions.text: He can always crack the whip if a wild-cat strike is 0 threatened

parts.words: He can always crack the whip if a wild-cat strike is 0 threatened
parts.note: a boss facing an unofficial strike, re-read as a circus performer facing an attack by big cats

explanation.surface: A tough manager who can bring workers to heel when an unofficial walkout looms.
explanation.walkthrough: A wildcat strike is an unofficial walkout; here it is a literal attack by a big cat, and cracking the whip is the circus act. The stray '0' is an OCR mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A circus performer who controls lions and tigers with a whip handles big cats.

clue.text: At heart I feel it isn't easy to grasp

indicators.note: at heart says the letters are taken from inside the words given

explanation.surface: Someone says that, deep down, they find something hard to understand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At heart' takes the inside of 'I feel'. The definition is the slippery fish's habit of escaping a grip.
explanation.definitionFit: A slippery fish is famously hard to hold, hence 'slippery as' this creature.

clue.text: A flier in embryo, possibly, wanted for poaching?

definitions.text: A flier in embryo, possibly, wanted for poaching?

parts.words: A flier in embryo, possibly, wanted for poaching
parts.note: a bird not yet hatched, and an item cooked in simmering water; poaching also hints at a criminal wanted

explanation.surface: A young pilot wanted by police for illegal hunting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanted for poaching' suggests a criminal; it means needed for the cooking method.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird's unhatched embryo sits in a shell that is also simmered in water at breakfast.

clue.text: Where the smoke goes up in Scotland?

definitions.text: Where the smoke goes up in Scotland?

parts.words: Where the smoke goes up in Scotland
parts.note: the Scots dialect word for a chimney

explanation.surface: A question about where Scottish smoke rises.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scots word for a chimney or flue.
explanation.definitionFit: Scots dialect names the flue or chimney stack by this short word.

clue.text: A matter for keen discussion, such as who fired the Reichstag?

definitions.text: A matter for keen discussion, such as who fired the Reichstag?

parts.words: A matter for keen discussion, such as who fired the Reichstag
parts.note: a hotly debated issue, and literally the unresolved question of who set fire to the German parliament in 1933

explanation.surface: A debate over who set the German parliament ablaze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fired' means set alight: the 1933 Reichstag fire's culprit is a debated issue that literally concerns burning.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotly debated, urgent issue is a pressing topic of the moment.

clue.text: Sticky sweet

definitions.meaning: a chewy confection such as a wine-...

explanation.definitionFit: The word names both an adhesive substance and a chewy confection.

clue.text: East Saxon nobleman naming a petrochemical product

parts.note: a thane was an Anglo-Saxon lord

explanation.surface: An East Saxon lord gives his name to an oil product.
explanation.definitionFit: A colourless hydrocarbon gas extracted from natural gas and oil refining is used in plastics.

clue.text: Two bills I put on a tree

indicators.note: two says the word for bills is written twice over

parts.note: AC, short for account, is a bill

explanation.surface: Two invoices pinned to a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorny tree of warm climates such as the wattle is a common genus of tree.

clue.text: A: distribution of arms to a 5 trouble spot in Ethiopia

indicators.note: distribution means the letters of arms are spread around into a new order

explanation.surface: Weapons handed out to a conflict zone in East Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distribution of' rearranges ARMS to SMAR. ASMARA, then in Ethiopia, is now the capital of Eritrea. The stray '5' is an OCR mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The city was at the centre of the Eritrean conflict when Eritrea was part of Ethiopia.

clue.text: Scattered tribes brown in colour

indicators.note: scattered means the letters of tribes are dispersed into a new order

explanation.surface: Dispersed peoples of a brown complexion.
explanation.definitionFit: A brownish pigment made from soot is a shade of brown used by artists.

clue.text: Suitable garb for one who wants to rocket to fame?

definitions.text: Suitable garb for one who wants to rocket to fame?

parts.words: Suitable garb for one who wants to rocket to fame
parts.note: rocketing to fame usually means rising fast, but here it is a literal rocket trip for an astronaut

explanation.surface: Advice on what to wear for a meteoric rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocket to fame' means rise quickly; read literally, the astronaut needs a pressurised outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: An astronaut's pressurised outfit is the clothing worn outside Earth's atmosphere.

clue.text: Famous. Dutch sailor man after week-end return

indicators.note: after puts the man piece following the other one
return means the abbreviation for the weekend day is read backwards

parts.note: Sat, Saturday, is a day of the weekend
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man comes back after the weekend.
explanation.walkthrough: Abel Tasman was the 17th-century Dutch explorer who gave his name to Tasmania; the full stop after 'Famous' is an OCR mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Abel Tasman was the Dutch navigator who reached Tasmania and New Zealand in 1642.

clue.text: Kind of folk who live by trading French sea songs?

definitions.text: Kind of folk who live by trading

parts.note: mer is French for sea
chants are songs

explanation.surface: Sea shanties from France sung by traders.
explanation.definitionFit: Traders who buy and sell goods for a living are dealers in commerce.

clue.text: A Verdi composition that's far from monotonous

indicators.note: composition means the letters of the opera composer's name are put together anew

explanation.surface: A piece by Verdi that is anything but dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Something full of diversity and change is the opposite of monotonous.

clue.text: Shaky start with a jewel meant to deceive the opposition

indicators.note: shaky means the letters of start are unsteady and fall into a new order

parts.note: a gem is a jewel

explanation.surface: A nervous beginning with a jewel to fool rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is adjectival in the surface but describes the scheme itself, a ruse meant to deceive.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruse or trick planned to outwit an enemy is a scheme designed to mislead.
